title: Delhi Dementia Conclave Urges Prevention, Caregiver Support as Cases Head Toward 17 Million
excerpt: Experts at the Hope for Dementia Conclave 2026 warned that dementia cases in India could nearly double to 16.9 million by 2036, calling for prevention, early diagnosis and caregiver support to become public health priorities.
body:
• Policymakers, clinicians and civil-society leaders at the Hope for Dementia Conclave 2026 in New Delhi urged India to put dementia prevention, earlier identification and caregiver support at the heart of its public health response to ageing.
  • A LASI-DAD study estimated 7.4 per cent of Indians aged 60 and above — about 8.8 million people — were living with dementia in 2023; demographic change could push that number to 16.9 million by 2036.
  • Chief guest Dr V.K. Paul said dementia should be treated as a public health challenge, tackled with both classical and technological tools while keeping "dignity and compassion" at the centre of care.
  • If an older relative shows persistent memory or behaviour changes, seek a medical assessment early — early identification gives families time to plan. Ayushman Arogya Mandirs were flagged at the conclave as community-level platforms where such support can reach families.

India must place dementia prevention, earlier identification and caregiver support at the heart of its public health response to ageing, policymakers, clinicians and civil-society leaders said at the Hope for Dementia Conclave 2026, held in New Delhi.

The conclave was organised by Hope Ek ASHA as the organisation marked 25 years of working with people living with dementia and their families. It brought together specialists in neurology, psychiatry, geriatrics, caregiver training and dementia services to discuss how India can prepare for a rapidly growing need for diagnosis, care and support.

8.8 million today, 16.9 million by 2036

The scale of the challenge is stark. A nationally representative LASI-DAD study published in Alzheimer's & Dementia in 2023 estimated that 7.4 per cent of Indians aged 60 years and older — approximately 8.8 million people — were living with dementia. Based on demographic change alone, and assuming prevalence remains unchanged, that number was projected to reach 16.9 million by 2036.

India is ageing fast, and the projections mean dementia will move from a private family struggle to a population-level health burden within a decade — one the country's health system is not currently built to absorb.

Prevention and early identification

Speakers at the conclave argued the response has to shift from treatment to overall brain health: preventing what can be prevented and identifying the condition far earlier than happens today. Addressing the gathering as chief guest, Dr V.K. Paul called for dementia to be treated as a public health challenge, responded to "through the tools that public health offers and can be crafted. Classical tools as well as technological tools."

"Dementia should be seen as a public health challenge... and never losing sight that the person in front, above all, is to be offered the highest level of dignity and compassion, and embracing the connection as a human being is at the heart of that journey."

— Dr V.K. Paul, chief guest, Hope for Dementia Conclave 2026

Paul pointed to Ayushman Arogya Mandirs — the country's network of community health and wellness centres — as platforms through which dementia awareness and early support could reach families where they live.

Caregivers carry the weight

A central theme of the conclave was the people who do most of dementia care in India: unpaid family members, overwhelmingly women. Caregiver training and support were framed not as add-ons but as core infrastructure — without them, diagnosis alone changes little for families.

Speakers stressed that care must keep dignity at its centre. "Embracing the connection as a human being is at the heart of that journey," Paul said, "even as we move to a public health paradigm."

Why it matters for NRIs

For the millions of Indians living abroad, dementia is often managed across continents — a parent in India, children in the US, UK or Canada coordinating doctors, caregivers and costs over video calls. The conclave's emphasis on early identification and trained caregiver support speaks directly to that reality: families who spot decline early and build a care plan have far more options than those forced to act in crisis.

What to watch

Whether the conclave's recommendations translate into policy will be the real test. Experts are looking for dementia to be folded into national health programmes, caregiver support to get dedicated funding, and community platforms like Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to take on screening and guidance roles. Hope Ek ASHA, marking 25 years, signalled it intends to stay at the centre of that push.
nri_angle: Millions of NRIs coordinate care for ageing parents in India from abroad; the conclave's push for early diagnosis, caregiver training and community-level support speaks directly to the logistics and costs of long-distance caregiving.
author: Diaspora Desk
